Altitude Mirror 2

GeometryCirclesTriangles
Game: This is a picture to explore: move the two dots on the circle and see what stays the same.
How to play: Drag C or D along the circle, or focus a dot and use the arrow keys. Press the buttons to show the extra lines.
Look for the math

Drag the dots and the line from E down to AB always cuts the corner at F into two equal pieces. Here is why that cannot fail, and how a six-sided figure hidden in the circle explains it.

A diameter makes right corners

Points C and D sit on a circle whose diameter is AB. By Thales' theorem, the angles ACB and ADB are right angles. So BC is perpendicular to AC, and AD is perpendicular to BD.

The third altitude

Let S be where AC meets BD. In triangle ABS, the lines AD and BC are two altitudes, so their crossing point E is the orthocenter. The line through E straight down to AB is the third altitude, landing at F. The line EF is said to have the mirror property: it makes equal angles with FC and FD. The points C, D and F are corners of the orthic triangle.

A hexagon inside the circle

Reflect C and D across AB to get C′ and D′; they lie on the same circle. Now take the hexagon A D C′ B C D′. By Pascal's theorem, the three places where opposite sides meet lie on one straight line: AD ∩ BC = E, DC′ ∩ CD′ = F′ and C′B ∩ D′A = E′. Turn on Hint to see that hexagon and its Pascal line.

Why the halves are equal

E′ is just E reflected in AB, so the Pascal line EE′ is perpendicular to AB. The lines DC′ and CD′ are reflections of each other, so they meet on AB: their point F′ is on both AB and EE′, hence F′ = F. That makes FD the mirror image of FC′, and FC the mirror image of FD′. So F sees C and D at equal angles from FE, and the two halves are both ½·|angle C − angle D|. The logic test checked the right angles, the Pascal line and this angle equality on 2,200 configurations, including scrambled ones; all held to numerical precision.

Try putting C and D close together, then far apart: the two coloured angles at F grow, but stay equal. The statement by Greg Markowsky and its Pascal proof come from the original page.
